chunks: "It depends which loss you look at, and what you compare against. Conduction loss is I squared R.

If I add phases and keep each phase's FETs and inductor the same, the total conduction loss falls like one over N, because each phase carries 1/N of the current and there are N of them: N times (I/N) squared is I squared over N.
So at high load efficiency goes up. But if I compare with a single phase built from the same total silicon, conduction loss is basically the same.
Switching loss in total is about the same, since each phase switches 1/N of the current at the same frequency.
Gate-drive loss and driver and core loss go up with the number of active phases, because they don't depend on load.
At light load that fixed overhead dominates, so a four-phase converter can be less efficient at 5 amps than a single phase.
The fix is phase shedding: the controller turns off phases as load drops so the efficiency stays high across the range.
There are also second-order wins: lower ripple per phase can mean lower AC losses in the inductors, and you can choose smaller faster FETs because each carries less current.
So in short: better at heavy load, worse at light load unless you shed phases, with the exact answer depending on parts."
